title: A fossil-competitive primary supply of multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated industrial process that uses CO2 as its carbon feedstock, water as its hydrogen source, and low-carbon energy to make a named multicarbon chemical at a cost competitive with its fossil-derived counterpart. Ethylene is the principal demonstrated chemical example in the supplied evidence. The target is a dependable primary supply of useful material, encompassing conversion, carbon recovery, purification and sustained production.

Multicarbon products contain two or more carbon atoms, so producing them from CO2 requires building carbon–carbon bonds as well as reducing the carbon feedstock. The supplied ethylene study demonstrates this chemical conversion in the laboratory. The proposed breakthrough would carry that capability through a complete production system whose energy use, carbon efficiency, durability, equipment requirements and product quality support competitive operation.

Scope synthesis: the concept is defined by the feedstocks, named product and integrated performance, rather than by a mandatory single reactor architecture. Direct electrochemical conversion and routes involving intermediate products could both qualify if the complete process met the same requirements. Success for ethylene would establish a supply route for ethylene; it would not automatically establish competitive production of other chemicals or liquid fuels.

significance.text: A competitive CO2-to-ethylene process would create an alternative carbon supply for an existing industrial product. The revolutionary change would lie in how the product is supplied: carbon that currently enters production through fossil feedstocks could instead enter through captured CO2. The reported laboratory conversion establishes a chemical basis for this conditional possibility, but does not establish its industrial competitiveness.

Conditional impact synthesis: wider adoption could reduce geological-carbon dependence in plastics, solvents and fuels, provided suitable product-specific processes were developed and deployed. That outcome also depends on the CO2 source. Reusing CO2 captured from a fossil-derived stream alone would not establish independence from geological carbon. A credible climate benefit would additionally require low-carbon energy and accounting for capture, conversion, purification and the product's eventual use or disposal.

The analogy to solar hydrogen has an important limit. Hydrogen production can provide an enabling input for some chemical routes, but it does not itself supply carbon-containing products or demonstrate carbon–carbon bond formation. The supplied outdoor hydrogen efficiency reports therefore illustrate progress in a related energy-conversion capability. Their different efficiency conventions and heating boundaries also prevent treating their percentages as a directly comparable progression toward multicarbon production.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is an integrated production system that combines selective conversion with competitive total performance. High faradaic efficiency means a large fraction of electrical charge produces the desired product; it does not, by itself, establish low electricity consumption, high utilization of incoming CO2, inexpensive purification or low production cost. These quantities must be reconciled across the complete process.

Concrete engineering barriers include maintaining product selectivity and useful current density over long operation, providing sufficient electrode area at acceptable cost, recovering carbon from process streams, and separating the desired product without erasing the conversion advantage. Pressure management must also be evaluated across the system. The ethylene study's energy argument concerns using captured CO2 at its existing pressure rather than first depressurizing and later repressurizing it; it does not establish that high pressure generally minimizes total energy consumption.

The economic barrier remains distinct from the laboratory chemistry. The reviewed supplementary analysis models a 100-tonne-per-day ethylene factory with a 20-year life and optimistic capital-cost assumptions, including the electrolyzer and pressure-swing adsorption unit. Such modeling can identify conditions under which a process might become attractive, but measured operation must establish whether conversion, separation, equipment life and auxiliary requirements can satisfy those conditions together.

Assessment boundary: the supplied evidence does not demonstrate the complete target. It also does not establish that no qualifying system exists anywhere as of 2026-11-01. The remaining breakthrough described here is the gap between the supplied achievements and the concept's integrated requirements; worldwide present-day absence remains unresolved.

current_state.text: Huang, Gao, Zhao and colleagues, published in Nature Catalysis on 28 August 2025, report up to 85% faradaic efficiency and an ethylene partial current density of 750 mA cm−2 at 20 bar. They also report stable electrolysis for more than 1,500 hours at 600 mA cm−2 and a proof-of-concept product stream brought to 99.9% ethylene purity. These are substantial laboratory achievements. The reported duration is roughly two months; the supplied account does not establish that every peak performance figure and the purification result were maintained together throughout that run.

The ethylene main article was available to the supplied review as a partial subscription preview containing the abstract, while the complete matching supplementary information was available. The supplement extends the evidence beyond the original abstract-only description and distinguishes laboratory separation work from projected factory economics. Its 100-tonne-per-day economic scenario is a model under optimistic assumptions, not an operating plant demonstration. Likewise, the energy conclusion addresses avoiding a depressurization–repressurization cycle for already pressurized captured CO2; it does not show achieved commodity displacement or a general minimum-energy operating pressure.

For hydrogen production, Zhang and colleagues' Science Advances paper, published on 26 February 2025, reports outdoor solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies of 29.1% at 95 mA cm−2 and 25.9% at 240 mA cm−2 in a photovoltaic–alkaline-electrolysis system. The supplied review had an identity-verified full article through an alternative-hosted PDF. It records external heating used to emulate heat that could be available in a larger system, and an efficiency calculation using a 1.23 V convention. These details qualify the interpretation of the reported efficiencies as complete-system energy performance.

A 2026 Communications Engineering paper by Martínez, Ohlmann, Smolinka and Dimroth reports an outdoor peak solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 31.3% for a Fraunhofer concentrator module. According to the full publisher PDF described in the supplied review, that figure uses hydrogen's higher heating value and excludes energy for preheating water to 60 °C. Improved thermal integration is proposed for a future design. The result therefore has a different accounting boundary from the Zhang study and should not be read as an unqualified efficiency improvement over it. Neither hydrogen experiment demonstrates multicarbon chemical production.

Evidence boundary: the supplied texts do not document the originally asserted complete photovoltaic–electrolyzer–syngas pilot chains or establish their deployment status. That evidentiary gap does not show that such chains do not exist. The supplied freshness-search record is empty, so these dated achievements cannot establish an exhaustive worldwide state of the field on 2026-11-01.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration milestone: continuously produce ethylene or a named liquid fuel from CO2 and water at tonne-per-day scale for thousands of hours, with measured output quality and independently checked energy and carbon balances. Report throughput, electrode area, operating pressure, durability, maintenance, auxiliary inputs and purification requirements. These are proposed criteria for a convincing integrated demonstration, not established published completion standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration milestone

completion_criteria.text: Proposed competitiveness assessment: identify the product and fossil comparator explicitly—for example, ethylene against a specified steam-cracking route, or a named fuel against its relevant incumbent route. Define what counts as beating that comparator in production cost, energy use and carbon performance, and disclose any tradeoffs. Use consistent boundaries that include CO2 sourcing and capture, compression, electricity and heat, water treatment, carbon recovery, separation and equipment replacement. Distinguish measured operating data from assumptions about future electricity prices, plant life, capital costs or scale.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed competitiveness assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: independently verify the balances and product measurements, and reproduce sustained performance in another run or independently operated installation. Test and report sensitivity to relevant feed impurities, operating conditions and interruptions. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. A tonne-per-day demonstration would be a milestone toward plant-scale competitiveness; additional evidence would be needed to substantiate commercial plant economics and reliable supply.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary

completion_criteria.text: A laboratory faradaic efficiency above 80% alone would not satisfy the integrated objective. The supplied ethylene study already reports up to 85%, while its factory economics remain modeled. Selectivity, useful throughput, total energy consumption, carbon recovery, product purification and operating life must therefore be demonstrated together at the claimed system boundary.
completion_criteria.label: A laboratory faradaic efficiency above 80% alone would

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-06, mild nitrogen fixation competitive with Haber–Bosch, and CHEMREV-12, selective methane-to-methanol conversion under mild conditions, are close comparisons because each targets a specific commodity process whose value depends on integrated performance. Their chemical tasks remain distinct: nitrogen fixation activates nitrogen, methane-to-methanol modifies an existing carbon feedstock, and CHEMREV-07 builds multicarbon products from CO2. CHEMREV-13, plastics returned to monomers below virgin-production cost and energy, instead recovers carbon already embodied in materials; it could complement a CO2-derived primary supply.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-01, predicting realistic chemical outcomes, and CHEMREV-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request, could aid catalyst discovery and process design for CO2 conversion. CHEMREV-04, on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules, and CHEMREV-11, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond, concern broader synthetic choice and selectivity. CHEMREV-07 can succeed for a named commodity without delivering arbitrary synthesis, general reaction prediction or general catalyst design.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-03, a manufacturable ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor, and CHEMREV-08, an aviation-relevant rechargeable air-breathing battery, concern electrical infrastructure or energy storage. They could influence the wider energy system supporting chemical production, but neither establishes competitive CO2 conversion. Solar hydrogen, although absent as a separate entry in the supplied roster, is another potential enabling technology; its demonstrated efficiencies do not satisfy CHEMREV-07's carbon-conversion requirements.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-09, phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids, could support development of catalysts, electrodes or separation materials. CHEMREV-10, positional manufacture of macroscopic atomically specified matter, targets a much broader level of manufacturing control than commodity chemical production requires. CHEMREV-02, open-ended Darwinian evolution in a synthetic chemical system, concerns sustained chemical evolution rather than industrial feedstock supply. These entries retain separate completion conditions even where future methods or materials might overlap.

change_log.change: Preserved CHEMREV-07's identity as an integrated, fossil-competitive supply of named multicarbon products.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent and significant despite limitations in particular supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad multi-month stability description with more than 1,500 hours, approximately two months, and separated the reported performance metrics.
change_log.reason: The numerical duration is more precise, and the supplied evidence does not establish simultaneous sustained operation at every reported peak metric.

change_log.change: Corrected the high-pressure energy interpretation to concern direct use of already pressurized captured CO2.
change_log.reason: The reviewed abstract compares this with depressurizing and repressurizing; it does not establish a universal energy advantage for high pressure.

change_log.change: Updated the ethylene evidence boundary from abstract only to a partial main-article preview plus complete matching supplementary information.
change_log.reason: The validated review includes the supplement, which supplies useful separation and economic-model detail without providing the complete main article.

change_log.change: Added the modeled 100-tonne-per-day factory scale, 20-year life and optimistic capital-cost assumptions.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish projected economic feasibility from demonstrated plant-scale operation.

change_log.change: Expanded the hydrogen results with operating current densities, external heating, efficiency conventions and excluded preheating energy.
change_log.reason: The full papers described in the review materially qualify the percentages and prevent a direct common-boundary comparison.

change_log.change: Made broader geological-carbon independence conditional on CO2 sourcing, product-specific processes and deployment.
change_log.reason: One competitive product and fossil-derived captured CO2 do not establish sector-wide independence from geological carbon.

change_log.change: Recast the asserted photovoltaic–electrolyzer–syngas pilot chains and worldwide absence of a qualifying plant as unresolved.
change_log.reason: The supplied texts do not substantiate the pilot-chain assertion, and the empty freshness record cannot establish worldwide present-day absence.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion milestone to include explicit comparator metrics, system boundaries, reproducibility and practical operating limits.
change_log.reason: Faradaic efficiency and pilot throughput alone cannot establish full-system competitiveness; proposed thresholds must remain distinct from established standards.

change_log.change: Added explicit overlap and distinctions across the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: Related enabling capabilities and complementary carbon routes should remain separate innovations with their own completion conditions.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system worldwide meets the integrated target as of 2026-11-01 remains unassessed by the supplied freshness record.

The supplied account does not establish whether the ethylene selectivity, peak partial current density, long-duration operation and product purification were demonstrated together under one sustained operating condition.
Measured plant-scale production costs, complete energy and carbon balances, equipment life and separation performance sufficient to establish fossil competitiveness are not supplied.
The named commercial comparator, CO2 source, electricity and heat assumptions, and required margins for cost, energy and carbon performance remain to be specified.
The original assertion about complete photovoltaic–electrolyzer–syngas pilot chains remains unsubstantiated within these inputs; this does not establish their absence.
The hydrogen efficiencies cannot be compared directly without harmonizing their heating-value conventions and thermal-energy boundaries.
The tonne-per-day and thousands-of-hours thresholds remain proposed milestones; evidence connecting them to commercial plant economics would still be required.
